golokdham-temple.desc: Golokdham Temple stands in Shaldanga village, about 12 km north-west of Debiganj upazila town. An inscription dates it to 1846, and it was built in memory of Golok Krishna Goswami, after whom it is named. The temple is hexagonal and stands on a high old platform, with one chamber inside. Its design shows a classical, Greek-like influence that is unusual for rural Bengal. Trees surround it, and the Department of Archaeology lists it as a protected monument.
blocks: How to get there
From Panchagarh go to Debiganj by bus, then take an auto or van about 12 km to Shaldanga.
Good to know
There are no facilities nearby. Ask locals in Shaldanga for directions.

glance: 410 km to Panchagarh by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
tetulia-kanchenjunga-view.desc: Tetulia sits on the Mahananda River at the very top of Bangladesh. From late October to early December, when the air is clear after the monsoon, the white peaks of Kanchenjunga become visible to the north, often turning pink at sunrise. The old dak bungalow on a rise above the river is a favourite viewpoint. Even without the mountains, the riverbank and the border villages make a peaceful place to stay.
blocks: How to get there
Buses run from Panchagarh town to Tetulia (about 1 hour); from Dhaka, overnight buses go to Panchagarh.
Good to know
Be up before sunrise; the view is clearest in the early morning and often fades by midday. Stay at least two nights to improve your chances.

tetulia-tea-gardens.desc: Unlike the hilly gardens of Sylhet, Panchagarh's tea grows on flat plains, a cultivation that took off from the late 1990s. Large estates and thousands of small farmers' plots now cover much of Tetulia upazila. Walking the paths between the bushes, you can watch pluckers at work and see shade trees lined up in rows. The green landscape with the border just beyond is unlike anywhere else in the country.
blocks: How to get there
Gardens line the roads around Tetulia; hire an auto-rickshaw or bicycle from Tetulia bazar.
Good to know
Ask permission before entering private estates. Plucking is busiest from spring to autumn.

glance: Markets in Panchagarh town and Tetulia in winter
panchagarh-malta-orange.desc: Panchagarh's cooler winters suit citrus, and farmers have planted orchards of oranges and green-skinned malta in recent years. The fruit is juicy and tangy, and some orchards welcome visitors in the harvest season. It is a small but growing part of the district's farming story, alongside tea. Buying from the orchard is the best way to taste it fresh.
blocks: Good to know
Ask locally which orchards are open to visitors.

glance: Tea stalls in Tetulia bazar and estate shops around Tetulia
panchagarh-tea.desc: Panchagarh is now one of Bangladesh's major tea regions, much of it grown by small farmers who sell fresh leaf to local factories. Some estates produce organic and orthodox teas alongside regular CTC. A cup of strong milk tea at a Tetulia stall, or a light green tea from a local estate, tastes better with the gardens in view. Packets make easy gifts to take home.
blocks: Good to know
Ask for locally produced leaf rather than national brands.

glance: autumn (Aug–Sep), late autumn (Oct–Nov), winter (Dec–Jan) and spring (Feb–Mar)
banglabandha-zero-point.desc: Banglabandha is the country's northernmost point and a land port for trade with India, Nepal and Bhutan. Visitors come to stand at the zero point and see the border gates and trucks crossing. The surrounding countryside is full of tea and stone-laden rivers. It makes a natural pair with a stay in Tetulia.
blocks: How to get there
About 17 km north of Tetulia by auto-rickshaw or bus.
Good to know
Access to the very edge can need permission from authorities; carry ID and follow border guards' instructions.

glance: 410 km to Panchagarh by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
bhitargarh.desc: North-east of Panchagarh town lie the remains of Bhitargarh, a large fortified settlement enclosed by earthen walls and moats. Local legend links it with a King Prithu, and archaeologists have uncovered brick structures, temples and pottery here. Large old ponds, including the Maharaja's Dighi, still dot the area. Much of it looks like ordinary farmland, which makes discovering the ramparts all the more intriguing.
blocks: How to get there
About 15 km from Panchagarh town; hire an auto-rickshaw and ask for Bhitargarh and Maharaja Dighi.
Good to know
Go with a local who knows the site, as there is little signage.

mahananda-stone-collectors.desc: The rivers of Panchagarh carry gravel and stones from the hills to the north, and gathering them has long been a livelihood here. Along the Mahananda near Tetulia, men and women stand in the cold, clear water sifting stones into baskets. The stones are sorted by size on the banks and sold for construction. It is hard, physical work and a striking sight in the morning light along the border river.
blocks: How to get there
Visible from the riverbank in Tetulia near the dak bungalow.
Good to know
Ask before photographing workers. Stay on the Bangladeshi bank; the river marks the border.

maharajar-dighi.desc: Maharajar Dighi lies at Bhitargarh in Amarkhana union, about 15 km from Panchagarh town. Tradition says it was dug in the reign of a King Prithu, whose fortified city once spread around it. With its banks the tank covers nearly 54 acres, about 800 yards long, and the earthen banks rise some 20 feet. The water stays 40–50 feet deep even in the dry season and is famously clear. Every Pohela Boishakh a large fair is held on its banks, and on other days it is a calm place for a walk under the trees.
blocks: How to get there
From Panchagarh town take an auto or CNG north-east to Bhitargarh/Amarkhana (about 15 km).
Good to know
Visit around Pohela Boishakh for the fair. Swimming is not advised as the tank is very deep.

mirzapur-shahi-mosque.desc: Mirzapur Shahi Mosque stands in Mirzapur village of Atwari upazila. A Persian inscription suggests it dates from the Mughal period, probably around 1656 during Shah Shuja's rule in Bengal, though local accounts differ on who built it. The building is about 40 feet long and 25 feet wide, with three domes in a row and corner minarets. Its front wall is the highlight, decorated with varied carving and painted motifs. It is a protected monument and still an active mosque.
blocks: How to get there
From Panchagarh town take a bus or CNG to Atwari, then an auto to Mirzapur; the Atwari Imambara is in the same union.
Good to know
Dress modestly and avoid prayer times. Morning light is best for the facade.

panchagarh-rocks-museum.desc: Housed at Panchagarh Government Women's College, this small museum was started by a teacher who gathered stones from the district's rivers and old sites. Its collection includes petrified wood, unusual rocks, ancient stone objects and household items of local communities. Many stones came from the Bhitargarh area. It is modest but unique in the country.
blocks: How to get there
In Panchagarh town; a short rickshaw ride to the women's college campus.
Good to know
Opening hours depend on the college; ask at the office.
